1170.title: Justice (ST II-II.58)
1170.howItsDone: Catholic teaching counts justice among the four cardinal virtues, describing it as the constant will to give God and neighbor their due, and Catholic social teaching applies it to wages, work and the common good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prudence: right reason applied to action, ending not in thinking but in doing. Your line was think, then act.

The neighbor's ladder has been leaning in the garage since spring. It was borrowed for one afternoon. Nobody's angry. Nobody's even asked for it back. But every time the garage door goes up, there it is, quietly saying something. Or a coworker's idea saved the project, and in the big meeting it somehow came out sounding like yours. Nobody lied, exactly. But something is owed and hasn't been paid. Today Thomas names the virtue that faces outward, toward everyone else. Justice.
screen: `A BORROWED LADDER, STILL HERE.` → `AN IDEA THAT WASN'T YOURS.` → `SOMETHING IS OWED.`

segments.voice: Thomas takes his definition from the old Roman lawyers and makes it his own. Justice is a habit by which a person, with a constant and lasting will, gives to each one their due. Look at the pieces. To each one: not just the people you like, or the ones who can pay you back. Their due: what belongs to them. Credit for their work. The truth. Wages on time. A fair hearing. Their ladder. Then the word that's easiest to skip: constant. One fair act on a good day isn't yet the virtue. Justice is being the kind of person who returns what's owed as a matter of course, the habit from two days ago, aimed outward. Here's what sets it apart. The other moral virtues, Thomas says, set a person right inside: calm when angry, brave when afraid. Justice is always about someone else. It's the virtue of the relationship; you can't do it alone in a room. And Thomas widens the circle as far as it goes. Even God is owed something: honor, worship, thanks. Jesus says it in one breath, in the Douay-Rheims: "Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's; and to God, the things that are God's." Justice, for Thomas, isn't first a courtroom or a protest sign, though it reaches both. It starts with the ladder in the garage.

segments.voice: Let the people around you come to mind one at a time: family, coworkers, a neighbor, the person who serves you coffee. For each, ask quietly whether there's something you owe and haven't given: thanks, credit, a returned call, money, an apology, a fair hearing for someone you've written off. Let the clearest one rise to the top, and if you pray, name that person before God.
Justice. For Thomas, a steady will to give each person what is their due, a virtue that always faces someone else. Today's word.

1171.title: Fortitude (ST II-II.123)
1171.hook: courage is mostly endurance, not attack
1171.howItsDone: Catholic teaching counts fortitude among the four cardinal virtues and among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and Catholics honor the martyrs as its highest witnesses while also praying for strength in illness, grief and ordinary trials.

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice: a steady will to give each person, and God, their due. Your line was each their due.

Two kinds of brave. The first runs into the burning building. It's sudden, loud, and it makes the evening news. The second sits in a plastic chair beside a hospital bed through a long night, and the next, and the next. Nobody films it. There's nothing to charge at, only staying. Ask the evening news which one is courage, and the first one wins. Ask Thomas Aquinas, and you get a different answer. After prudence and justice comes the third of the cardinal virtues. Fortitude.
screen: `THE BURNING BUILDING.` → `THE PLASTIC CHAIR, NIGHT AFTER NIGHT.` → `WHICH ONE IS COURAGE?`

segments.voice: Fortitude, for Thomas, keeps a person steady in the good when fear pushes them to quit. It deals with two things: fear, which makes us want to run, and daring, which can make us reckless. Fortitude holds the line between them. Then his surprising claim. Its main act isn't attacking. It's enduring: standing firm. His reasons: when you attack, you're usually the stronger one in that moment; when you endure, something stronger is pressing on you. Attack looks to a danger still ahead; endurance faces one already here. And attack can be over in a flash, while endurance has to last. So staying is often harder than charging. The plastic chair, not the burning building. Thomas has in mind above all the gravest dangers, standing firm even before death, and he calls martyrdom the highest act of this virtue. The Catechism describes fortitude more broadly, as firmness in difficulties and constancy in pursuing the good. That widens it to ordinary life: the long illness, the job you can't leave yet, the child who isn't sleeping, the grief that won't hurry. Jesus says in the Douay-Rheims: "but he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved." Persevere. Not win. Last. And fortitude isn't the absence of fear. Thomas assumes the fear is there; that's what the virtue is for. A person with fortitude feels the full weight, and doesn't put down the good thing they're carrying.

1172.title: Temperance (ST II-II.141)
1172.hook: moderation gives a kind of beauty to a life
1172.howItsDone: Catholics practice temperance in ordinary meals and drinks, and the Church sets days of fasting and abstinence, such as the Fridays of Lent; the Catechism teaches temperance as one of the cardinal virtues.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fortitude: for Thomas, courage is mostly staying put under a hard thing, not charging at it. Your line was endure.

Somewhere past the middle of a bag of chips, the chips stop tasting like much. The hand keeps going anyway. The pleasure left a while back, and the eating carried on without it. Same with a show at one in the morning, or a phone in bed. Nobody decides to overdo it. It just keeps rolling. Thomas Aquinas has a name for the virtue that catches that moment, and he says something odd about it. He doesn't call it grim, or strict. He calls it beautiful. Today's word is temperance.
screen: `THE CHIPS STOP TASTING LIKE MUCH.` → `THE HAND KEEPS GOING.` → `THOMAS CALLS IT BEAUTIFUL.`

segments.voice: For Thomas, temperance keeps a steady hand on the pleasures closest to the body: eating, drinking, and sex. These pull hardest, he says, because they're tied to keeping life going. Then the first surprise. Thomas does not think less pleasure is always better. He names a vice on the other side, insensibility: refusing pleasure so far that you neglect what your body and life actually need. Despising a good meal is not, for him, a virtue. Temperance isn't hating pleasure. It's enjoying it in the right measure. And the measure? What life needs, and what fits your situation, your work, the people around you. A wedding feast and a Tuesday lunch have different measures, and both can be temperate. Now the second surprise. Beauty belongs to temperance in a special way. Beauty, for Thomas, has to do with clarity and right proportion. The pleasures temperance looks after are the ones that, left unchecked, cloud a person's reason, the very thing that lets a human life shine. Temperance keeps that light on. So a temperate life isn't cramped. It's well-proportioned, like a room where nothing crowds out anything else. The Book of Wisdom names it beside its sister virtues, in the Douay-Rheims: "she teacheth temperance, and prudence, and justice, and fortitude." And Paul brings it to the kitchen table: "whether you eat or drink, or whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God." Eating isn't a distraction from God. It's one more place to give glory.
screen: `THE PLEASURES CLOSEST TO THE BODY.` · `TOO LITTLE IS A VICE TOO.` · `THE MEASURE: WHAT LIFE NEEDS.` · `BEAUTY: CLARITY AND PROPORTION.` · then, large: `WHETHER YOU EAT OR DRINK.`

segments.voice: Choose something small you can have now or soon, coffee or tea, a piece of fruit, a few squares of chocolate, and decide before you start how much is enough. Take it slowly, actually taste it, and notice the moment the pleasure is full; stop there, without punishing yourself and without pushing past it. If you pray, give thanks for it, in your own words or a grace you already know.
Temperance. For Thomas, the virtue that enjoys the body's pleasures in the right measure: not too much, and not too little, which gives a life its proportion. Today's word.
Your line: enough is beautiful. The right measure gives a life its shape. Same time tomorrow.

1173.title: Charity is friendship (ST II-II.23.1)
1173.hook: Thomas calls charity friendship with God
1173.howItsDone: Catholics speak of charity as the greatest of the theological virtues, and the Catechism, following Thomas, describes it as the virtue by which people love God above all things and their neighbor for the love of God, and, with St. Teresa of Avila, describes prayer as a close sharing between friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, temperance: the right measure of the body's pleasures, which Thomas says gives a life its beauty. Your line was enough is beautiful.

"I will not now call you servants." Jesus says it at the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, the night before he dies. "But I have called you friends." A servant does what he's told without being let in on the plan. A friend gets told things. Thomas Aquinas takes that one word, friends, very seriously. Back on day three hundred thirteen, charity, the love that never falls away, was the greatest of the three. When Thomas comes to it, his first question isn't whether it's a feeling, or a duty. He asks whether charity is friendship. His answer is today's title.

Thomas borrows Aristotle's account of friendship, in three parts. First, not every love is friendship. People love wine, Thomas says, but nobody is friends with wine. You want it for yourself; you don't wish it well. Friendship means wanting good for the other, for their sake. Second, that good will goes both ways. A one-sided love isn't yet a friendship. Third, friends share something: a life, a work, a table. Now Thomas lays this over God. Does God wish us well, for our sake? Yes. Is the love returned? It can be. And what's shared? God shares his own happiness with us. Thomas points to Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is faithful: by whom you are called unto the fellowship of his Son." So charity, for Thomas, is friendship between a person and God. Here's what makes it bold. Aristotle doubted friendship could stretch across a gap as wide as the one between people and gods. And Thomas raises a sharp objection against himself: friends live together, and we don't live with God. His answer: we do, already, in part. Paul again: "But our conversation is in heaven." In that old English, conversation means the way you live, where you belong. Begun here, finished later. One more turn. Because a friend loves what belongs to the friend, charity reaches everyone God loves, even enemies, the way you'd care for a friend's children, for the friend's sake. Charity is not a mood. It's a friendship with a wide circle.

segments.voice: Friends don't make speeches; they say what happened, what's bothering them, what made them laugh. Charity is friendship. For Thomas, charity is not only kindness. It's a friendship between a person and God, built on the happiness God shares. Today's word.

1174.title: What law is (ST I-II.90.4)
1174.hook: an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by the one who has care of the community
1174.howItsDone: Catholic social teaching draws on Thomas's account of law and the common good, and the Catechism teaches that authority is legitimate when it seeks the common good by morally acceptable means.

A red light, very late at night. No cars in any direction, no camera, nobody on the sidewalk. The light stays red, and a driver sits there anyway, drumming on the wheel, feeling slightly ridiculous. Why wait? Fear? Habit? Or because the rule is actually for something? Thomas Aquinas wanted to know what makes a rule a law at all, and not just somebody's order with a penalty attached. He packed his answer into one sentence, and that sentence is today.
screen: `A RED LIGHT, NOBODY AROUND.` → `WHY WAIT?` → `WHAT MAKES A RULE A LAW?`

segments.voice: Here's the sentence, in plain English. Law is an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by the one who has care of the community, and made known. A piece at a time. First, reason. A law isn't just a strong will. If a ruler's command isn't measured by reason, Thomas says, it's closer to wrongdoing than to law. A law points actions toward an end. Second, the common good: the good of the whole community, not one person's advantage, not even the lawmaker's. Third, the one who has care of the community. Making law belongs to the whole people, or to someone who stands in for them and looks after them. Fourth, it has to be made known. A law nobody could ever learn binds nobody. And that piece has a lovely turn: the deepest law, the natural law, was made known when God placed it in human minds. Now the edge of the sentence. If a rule serves the ruler against the people, Thomas says it's more like violence than law. He doesn't say every such rule may be ignored on the spot; sometimes it's wiser to bear it than to cause greater harm. But it isn't law in the full sense. In Proverbs, in the Douay-Rheims, wisdom speaks: "By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree just things." So for Thomas, law isn't the enemy of freedom. A good law is reason, handed to a community, so people can live well together.

1175.title: Do good, avoid evil (ST I-II.94.2)
1175.hook: the first principle of the natural law
1175.howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching speaks of a natural law that human reason can know, and the Catechism, drawing on Thomas, describes it as the light of understanding placed in us by God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what law is: an ordinance of reason for the common good. Your line was reason for the common good.

Two sisters at a kitchen table are arguing about whether to tell their cousin the hard truth about her new boyfriend. One says tell her now. The other says wait, it isn't our place. But underneath sits one thing neither says out loud, because neither needs to: both are trying to find the good thing to do. Nobody at that table argues for the bad option. Thomas Aquinas would call that buried agreement the first principle at work.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT AT THE KITCHEN TABLE.` → `THEY DISAGREE ABOUT NEARLY EVERYTHING.` → `BOTH WANT THE GOOD THING.`

segments.voice: Where does the natural law start? Thomas compares two kinds of thinking. When we think about what is, the first rule is that a thing can't both be and not be at the same time; every other argument leans on that. When we think about what to do, there has to be a first rule too, and Thomas finds it in the meaning of good. Good is what things seek. So the first principle of the practical mind is this: good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided. It sounds almost too simple. That's the point. It isn't a conclusion you argue your way to; it's known in itself, like knowing a whole is bigger than its part. Back on day three hundred ten, conscience said the same words: do good, avoid evil. Everything else in the natural law hangs from it. Thomas shows how it unfolds, from what people are drawn to by nature. Like everything that exists, we're drawn to keep on living. Like the animals, to bring up our young. As reasoning creatures, to know the truth about God and to live with others in society. So the natural law says: protect life, care for children, shun ignorance, don't harm the people you live among. Thomas leans on a line from the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "The light of thy countenance O Lord, is signed upon us." He reads it as the light of reason, stamped on us like a seal. Paul says people without the written law "shew the work of the law written in their hearts." For Thomas, the moral life doesn't start with a rulebook. It starts with a light already on.

1176.title: Grace (ST I-II.109–114)
1176.hook: we need God's help both to know and to do the good fully
1176.howItsDone: Catholics speak of grace as God's free gift, received especially through prayer and the sacraments, and the Church teaches that even the first turning toward God is moved by grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, do good, avoid evil: Thomas's first principle, a light already on in the mind. Your line was the first principle.

A couch is wedged in a doorway, one arm through, one arm stuck. The person moving it has pushed, lifted, tilted. It isn't that they're weak. They got it down the hall alone, and up the porch steps. But there's a point where one person, however strong, can't finish the job. Then a neighbor walks by, grabs the other end, says pivot, and the couch slides through. If the light of right and wrong is already on in us, is the light enough? Thomas's answer is grace.
screen: `A COUCH STUCK IN THE DOORWAY.` → `STRONG, BUT NOT ENOUGH.` → `IS THE LIGHT ENOUGH?`

segments.voice: Thomas opens his treatise on grace with a careful question: what can a person do without it? The answer is not nothing. People can know many true things by the natural light of the mind. Even after the fall, they can do some particular goods by their own powers. His examples are wonderfully ordinary: building houses, planting vineyards. Then the turn. Some good is not the whole good. Thomas compares fallen human nature to a sick person who can move around a little, but can't move freely until medicine heals him. So grace does two jobs. It heals what's wounded, and it lifts us toward a good beyond our nature: friendship with God, the charity of three days ago. No amount of pushing gets the couch through that door alone. Even turning toward God in the first place, even getting ready for grace, is itself God's help at work. Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "For it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will." And Jesus, in John: "without me you can do nothing." One line from the very start of the Summa keeps this from sounding grim: grace does not destroy nature, Thomas says, but perfects it. Grace isn't God shoving us aside to do the job himself. It's the other end of the couch. Back on day three hundred eight, it was free, not earned. Justice, fortitude, temperance, charity: each is something a person grows in. Today Thomas names the help underneath them.
screen: `NOT NOTHING: HOUSES AND VINEYARDS.` · `SOME GOOD IS NOT THE WHOLE GOOD.` · `GRACE HEALS AND LIFTS.` · `GRACE PERFECTS NATURE.` · then, large: `WITHOUT ME YOU CAN DO NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Pick the next real task in front of you, a hard email, a meal to cook, a conversation, a shift at work, and notice honestly, without shame, where your own strength runs out in it. If you pray, ask God for help with that task before you start, in your own words or a prayer you know; if you don't, think of one person you could ask, and let yourself be willing.
Grace. For Thomas, God's free help, which heals human nature and lifts it toward a good beyond its reach, without destroying it. Today's word.
